nodes.title: Electric Charge, Valence & Coulomb Forces
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2: Electric Charge, Field, and Potential; Lecture 1a Slides 7-16
nodes.summary: Atomic origin of charge (protons, electrons, valence ions Na+, K+, Cl-, Proteins P-), charge conservation, macroscopic charge neutrality in ICF/ECF, and electrostatic attraction/repulsion via F = qE.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does separating a tiny fraction of Na+ and Cl- across a 7.5 nm membrane create a strong electric field while the bulk ICF and ECF remain nearly charge neutral?

verification.question: In BITSEY's default cell (sim.py), initial intracellular concentrations are [Na+]=10, [K+]=125, [Cl-]=55, and [P-]=80 mol/m^3. What is the net bulk charge concentration sum(z_i * [ion_i]) at t=0?
options: 0 mol/m^3 (bulk charge neutral: 10 + 125 - 55 - 80 = 0)
+50 mol/m^3 (net positive intracellular fluid)
-55 mol/m^3 (dominated by chloride ions)
+270 mol/m^3 (sum of all ion concentrations)
verification.explanation: Bulk intracellular and extracellular fluids are macroscopically charge neutral: (+1)(10) + (+1)(125) + (-1)(55) + (-1)(80) = 0 mol/m^3. Even a tiny deviation (< 0.03 mol/m^3) produces tens of millivolts across the membrane.
verification.last_verified_output: ICF net charge = 0.0 mol/m^3, ECF net charge = 0.0 mol/m^3 (bulk neutral)

nodes.title: Electric Potential, Work & Relative Voltage
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2: Electric Potential Energy & Voltage; Lecture 1a Slides 15-18; EN01 Lecture 1 Slides 4-11
nodes.summary: Definition of voltage as potential energy difference per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C), why voltage is always relative to a reference (ECF ground = 0 V), and how ion pumps perform work against an electric field.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: If V_mem = -70 mV with ECF defined as ground (0 V), how much electrostatic work is required to move one mole of Na+ (z = +1) from ICF to ECF?

verification.question: If a cell membrane has thickness t_m = 7.5 nm and resting potential V_mem = -75 mV (with ECF = 0 V), what is the magnitude of the electric field |E| = |V_mem| / t_m inside the membrane?
options: 75 V/m
verification.explanation: |E| = 0.075 V / 7.5e-9 m = 1.0e7 V/m (10 million Volts per meter!). Because the lipid bilayer is only 7.5 nm thick, a 75 mV biological voltage creates an enormous electric field.
verification.last_verified_output: |E| = 1.00e+07 V/m across 7.5 nm bilayer

nodes.title: Electric Current & Membrane Capacitance
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2 & EE Intro: Current & Capacitors; Backgrounders Quiz Q1b; Sam & Max Problems Slides 14-19
nodes.summary: Current as rate of charge flow (I = dQ/dt), conventional current direction for positive vs. negative ions, and parallel-plate capacitor relations (Q = C*V) for the lipid bilayer membrane.
equations: I = dQ / dt = z * F * J_ion * A_cell
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Backgrounders Quiz: How much charge (in Coulombs) is stored on a 50 nF capacitor at 100 mV? How does adding a thick myelin sheath (series capacitance) change total membrane capacitance?

verification.question: Backgrounders Placement Quiz Q1b: How much charge Q (in Coulombs) is stored on a 50 nF capacitor when 100 mV is applied across it?
options: 5 nC (5.0e-9 Coulombs)
500 nC (5.0e-7 Coulombs)
verification.last_verified_output: Q = 5.00 nC on 50 nF capacitor at 100 mV

nodes.title: Ohm's Law, Conductance & Circuit Elements
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy EE: Circuit Analysis; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 2-3, 7-8, 12; Backgrounders Quiz Q1a
nodes.summary: Ideal voltage sources (batteries), ideal current sources (ion pumps), linear resistors (ion channels), Ohm's Law (V = IR), and reciprocal conductance (G = 1/R, I = GV).
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Backgrounders Quiz: How much current flows through a 20 Ohm resistor with 100 mV across it, in amps and in mA?

verification.question: Backgrounders Placement Quiz Q1a: How much current flows through a 20 Ohm resistor with 100 mV across it, and what is the resistor's conductance G?
options: I = 5 mA (0.005 A) and G = 0.05 S (1/Ohm)
I = 2 A and G = 20 S
I = 200 mA and G = 0.5 S
I = 0.2 mA and G = 0.005 S
verification.explanation: By Ohm's Law, I = V / R = 0.100 V / 20 Ohm = 0.005 A = 5 mA. Conductance is G = 1 / R = 1 / 20 = 0.05 S.

nodes.title: KVL, KCL, Series/Parallel & Voltage/Current Dividers
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2 & EE: Kirchhoff's Laws; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 4-11; Sam & Max Problems Slides 4-13
nodes.summary: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (sum of potential drops around any closed loop is zero), Kirchhoff's Current Law (sum of currents entering a node is zero), series/parallel resistor combinations, and voltage/current dividers.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In a two-resistor voltage divider between V_1 = +80 mV (R_1 = 40 Ohm) and V_2 = -80 mV (R_2 = 10 Ohm), why does the middle node voltage settle much closer to -80 mV?

verification.question: Circuits Backgrounder Slide 14: Two Nernst batteries V_1 = +80 mV (through R_1 = 40 Ohm) and V_2 = -80 mV (through R_2 = 10 Ohm) connect to node V_3. By KCL, what voltage does V_3 settle to?
options: -48 mV (pulled 4x closer to -80 mV because R_2 is 4x smaller than R_1)
0 mV (exact midpoint between +80 mV and -80 mV)
+48 mV (pulled toward the larger 40 Ohm resistor)
-64 mV
verification.last_verified_output: Divider node V_3 = -48.00 mV

nodes.title: Nodal Analysis of Multi-Branch Cell Circuits
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy EE: Nodal Analysis; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 14-17; Backgrounders Quiz Part 2 Q1-Q2
nodes.summary: Applying KCL at the intracellular fluid (ICF) node with parallel Nernst batteries (V_N,Na, V_N,K, V_N,Cl), channel conductances (G_Na, G_K, G_Cl), and Na+/K+ pump current sources to solve for V_mem analytically and intuitively.
equations: G_Na*(V_mem - V_N,Na) + G_K*(V_mem - V_N,K) + G_Cl*(V_mem - V_N,Cl) + I_pump,Na + I_pump,K = 0
V_mem = (G_Na*V_N,Na + G_K*V_N,K + G_Cl*V_N,Cl - I_pump,net) / (G_Na + G_K + G_Cl)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Backgrounders Quiz Part 2: Given V_N,Na=77mV (G=0.4), V_N,K=-89mV (G=2.2), V_N,Cl=-71mV (G=0.4), I_Na=60, I_K=-40, compute V_ICF. What happens if G_K becomes 100x larger?

verification.question: Backgrounders Placement Quiz Part 2: Given V_N,Na = +77 mV (G_Na = 0.4), V_N,K = -89 mV (G_K = 2.2), V_N,Cl = -71 mV (G_Cl = 0.4), and outward pump currents I_Na = 60, I_K = -40, what is V_ICF (and what if G_K becomes 100x larger)?
options: V_ICF = -71.13 mV; if G_K -> 220, V_ICF approaches V_N,K = -89 mV
V_ICF = -27.7 mV; if G_K -> 220, V_ICF approaches 0 mV
V_ICF = +77.0 mV; if G_K -> 220, V_ICF approaches +77 mV
V_ICF = -89.0 mV; if G_K -> 220, V_ICF approaches -71 mV
verification.explanation: KCL at ICF (Lecture 1b Slide 36): 0.4(V - 77) + 2.2(V + 89) + 0.4(V + 71) + 60 - 40 = 0 => 3.0*V + 213.4 = 0 => V = -71.13 mV. When G_K becomes 100x larger, the K+ branch dominates and pins V_ICF to V_N,K = -89 mV.
verification.last_verified_output: V_ICF = -71.13 mV; at 100x G_K -> -88.76 mV (approaches V_N,K = -89 mV)

nodes.title: Thevenin/Norton Equivalents & RC Delay Dynamics
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy EE: Thevenin's Theorem & RC Circuits; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 18-25
nodes.summary: Collapsing a multi-channel single-cell circuit into a single Thevenin voltage (V_th) and resistance (R_th) to analyze multicellular gap-junction networks and RC membrane charging time constants (tau = R_th * C_mem).
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: How does replacing each cell's 5-branch circuit with its Thevenin equivalent simplify solving for V_mem across two cells coupled by a gap-junction resistor R_GJ?

verification.question: In Circuits Backgrounder Slides 18-25, when we collapse a cell's parallel conductances (G_Na = 0.4, G_K = 2.2, G_Cl = 0.4 S) into a single Thevenin equivalent to compute RC charging delay, what is G_th = 1 / R_th?
options: G_th = G_Na + G_K + G_Cl = 3.0 S (so R_th = 1/3 Ohm and tau = R_th * C_mem)
G_th = G_K - G_Na = 1.8 S
G_th depends only on the Na+/K+ pump current
verification.explanation: Parallel conductances add directly: G_th = G_Na + G_K + G_Cl = 0.4 + 2.2 + 0.4 = 3.0 S. The RC time constant governing how fast V_mem slews to QSS is tau = C_mem / G_th.
verification.last_verified_output: G_th = 3.00 S, R_th = 0.3333 Ohm

nodes.title: Exponential Relaxation ODEs & 2D Vector Projections
nodes.source_material: Tufts MATH 32 Prereq; Lab 4 (Neuron HH ODEs); Lecture 3 Slide 25 (Vector Math Review)
nodes.summary: First-order linear ODEs for channel gating relaxation dx/dt = (x_inf - x)/tau, Hill function non-linearities, and 2D vector addition / dot-product projections for cardiac dipole leads.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: If m(0) = 0.4 and m_inf suddenly jumps to 0.9 with tau_m = 10 ms, write the trajectory m(t) and compare its initial slope to tau_m = 20 ms.

verification.question: In Sim Lab 4 (slab_neurons.pdf Slide 3), gating variable m obeys dm/dt = (m_inf - m)/tau_m. If m(0) = 0.4 and m_inf steps to 0.9 with tau_m = 10 s, what is m(10 s)?
options: 0.900 (reaches 100% in one time constant)
0.650 (linear midpoint)
verification.explanation: After one time constant t = tau_m, an exponential relaxation covers (1 - e^-1) approx 63.21% of the step: 0.4 + (0.9 - 0.4)*(1 - 0.3679) = 0.716.

nodes.title: Python, NumPy Vectorization & BITSEY Architecture
nodes.source_material: EN 01 Python Lectures; EE 123 sim.py, sim_toolbox.py, edebug.py, eplot.py
nodes.summary: Using Python, Thonny, and NumPy 2D arrays cc_cells[n_ions, n_cells] and Dm_array[n_ions, n_cells] to simulate ion fluxes, adaptive explicit vs. BDF implicit ODE integration, and Gate objects in BITSEY.
equations: V_mem = F * sum_i(z_i * cc_cells[i]) * V_cell / (A_cell * C_m)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In BITSEY's sim.py, why are all ion fluxes (pumps, channels, and gap junctions) normalized per m^2 of total cell membrane area before multiplying by cell_sa / cell_vol?

verification.question: In BITSEY's sim.py (compute_Vm), given a spherical cell of radius r = 5 um, patch capacitance c_m = 0.05 F/m^2, and Faraday constant F = 96485 C/mol, how many millivolts does V_mem change per +1 mol/m^3 of net uncompensated valence-1 charge?
options: Approx +3,216 mV (+3.22 V) per mol/m^3
Approx +26 mV per mol/m^3
Approx +1.0 mV per mol/m^3
Approx +100 mV per mol/m^3
verification.explanation: From sim.py line 375: scale = F * (V_cell / A_cell) / c_m = F * (r / 3) / c_m = 96485 * (5e-6 / 3) / 0.05 = 3.216 Volts = 3216 mV per (mol/m^3)!
verification.last_verified_output: BITSEY dV_mem / d[rho] = 3216.17 mV per (mol/m^3)

nodes.title: Central Dogma, Transcription Factors & Gene Logic
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4a: Biology Backgrounder (4a_bio_backgrounder.pptx Slides 1-25)
nodes.summary: The cell as a hardware/software machine: DNA bases/codons as software, transcription (DNA -> mRNA) and translation (mRNA -> tRNA/ribosome -> folded proteins), promoters as conditional if-then statements, and transcription factors (TFs) forming gene regulatory networks (GRNs).
equations: DNA (4^3 = 64 codons) -> mRNA -> Protein (20 amino acids)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: If every cell in your body has the exact same DNA software, how do promoters and transcription factors allow a toe cell and an eye cell to express completely different proteins?

verification.question: In Lecture 4a (Bio Backgrounder) & Lecture 4c (sim.py Hill_gate), what is the output of a Hill inverter H_inv([M]) = 1 / (1 + ([M]/K_M)^N) when the ligand concentration [M] exactly equals K_M, for any Hill coefficient N > 0?
options: 0.5 (the half-maximal switching threshold, regardless of N)
1.0 (fully open)
0.0 (fully closed)
verification.explanation: When [M] = K_M, ([M]/K_M)^N = 1^N = 1, so H_inv(K_M) = 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.5 for every N. Increasing N steepens the slope (gain) around K_M without shifting the 50% point.
verification.last_verified_output: Hill inverter H_inv(K_M) = 0.500 across N in {1, 2, 5, 10}

nodes.title: Fick's Law of Diffusion & Skittles Lab
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 21-28; Lecture 2a Slide 6; Real Lab 1: Skittles Diffusion (lab_skittles.pdf)
nodes.summary: Thermal random walk of particles, Fick's First Law (j_diff = -D dC/dx), why diffusion time scales quadratically with distance (t ~ L^2 / D), and why macroscopic organisms cannot rely on pure diffusion for long-range signaling.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Lab 1 Question: Why does diffusing over twice the distance take 4x as much time, and why do colored zones in the Skittles experiment form sharp boundaries initially?

verification.question: Real Lab 1 (Skittles Diffusion) Q4 & Lecture 2a Slide 6: If diffusing a chemical signal across 10 um takes 0.05 seconds, how long does it take to diffuse across a 10x larger distance (100 um)?
options: 5.0 seconds (10^2 = 100x longer because t_diff scales with distance squared, L^2)
0.5 seconds (10x longer, linear scaling)
0.05 seconds (independent of distance)
50 seconds (10^3 = 1000x longer)
verification.explanation: Because random-walk mean-squared displacement obeys <x^2> = 2*D*t, diffusing n times farther takes n^2 times longer. Over 1 meter (a human leg), diffusion would take years—which is why large animals evolved bioelectricity!

nodes.title: Ion Drift Flux, Mobility & Membrane Ohm's Law
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 29-40
nodes.summary: Electrostatic drift of ions in a membrane electric field (E = V_mem/L), terminal drift velocity from viscous drag (v = mu * f = mu * z * q * V_mem / L), Einstein relation (mu = D / k_B T), and microscopic derivation of Ohm's Law.
equations: j_drift = -C_ion * v_drift = -C_ion * mu_ion * z * q * (V_mem / L)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does a constant electric field produce a constant ion drift velocity rather than constant acceleration across the ion channel?

verification.question: Lecture 1a Slides 33-38: Using the Einstein relation mu = D / (k_B * T), why do ions moving through a membrane channel under a constant voltage V_mem reach a constant terminal drift velocity v_drift = mu * q * (V_mem / L)?
options: Viscous drag from water/channel collisions balances the electric force f = qE, just like air drag on a car
The electric field drops to zero inside the channel
Ions run out of kinetic energy halfway through the membrane
Magnetic fields cancel the electric acceleration
verification.explanation: In the crowded nanoworld, friction/drag is proportional to velocity. Terminal velocity is reached almost instantaneously where drag equals electrostatic force f = q*V_mem/L, giving Ohm's Law I = G*V.
verification.last_verified_output: Mobility u = D/(k_B*T) = 2.337e+02 m/(N*s) at T=310 K

nodes.title: Semi-Permeable Membranes & The Nernst Equation
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 41-59
nodes.summary: Equilibrium potential where inward/outward diffusion flux exactly balances electrostatic drift flux (j_diff + j_drift = 0), deriving the Nernst potential V_Nernst, and computing V_N for Na+ (+57 mV), K+ (-78 mV), and Cl- (-62 mV) in giant squid axons.
equations: V_Nernst = (R * T) / (z * F) * ln([ion]_ECF / [ion]_ICF) approx (26 mV / z) * ln([ion]_ECF / [ion]_ICF)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In a cell resting at V_mem = -60 mV, why does Cl- satisfy the Nernst equation (drift balances diffusion), whereas Na+ has both drift and diffusion pointing inward?

verification.question: Lecture 1a Slides 51-53 (Giant Squid In-Class Exercise): Given [K+]_ICF = 400 mM, [K+]_ECF = 20 mM and [Na+]_ICF = 50 mM, [Na+]_ECF = 440 mM at body temperature (RT/F approx 26 mV), what are V_Nernst,K and V_Nernst,Na?
options: V_N,K approx -78 mV and V_N,Na approx +57 mV
V_N,K approx +78 mV and V_N,Na approx -57 mV
V_N,K approx -62 mV and V_N,Na approx 0 mV
V_N,K approx -26 mV and V_N,Na approx +26 mV
verification.last_verified_output: Squid Nernst: V_K=-77.9 mV, V_Na=+56.5 mV, V_Cl=-61.8 mV

nodes.title: Na+/K+-ATPase Pumps, Detailed Balance vs. Steady State
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 60-81; sim_toolbox.py (GHK & pumpNaKATP)
nodes.summary: Active transport via the Na+/K+-ATPase pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed), distinguishing thermodynamic equilibrium (detailed balance, Cl-) from energy-consuming Steady State (SS, where j_channel + j_pump = 0 for each ion individually), and the linear vs. GHK flux models.
equations: j_total,i = G_i * (V_mem - V_N,i) + j_pump,i = 0 (for each ion i in SS)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Explain the difference between equilibrium (detailed balance) and steady state in a living cell: which ions are in equilibrium and which are only in steady state?

verification.question: Lecture 1a Slides 57-63: In a resting cell at Steady State (SS), why does Cl- satisfy detailed balance (j_drift + j_diff = 0) while Na+ and K+ do not?
options: Cl- has no active pump, so its channel flux must be zero at SS (V_mem = V_N,Cl); Na+ and K+ have an ATPase pump balancing non-zero channel leaks
Cl- channels are permanently closed in all living cells
Na+ and K+ cannot diffuse through ion channels
Cl- has valence z = 0
verification.explanation: Because Cl- has no pump in our model, steady state (d[Cl-]/dt = 0) requires its net channel current (drift + diffusion) to be zero, meaning V_mem settles to V_N,Cl. For Na+ and K+, passive channel leak is balanced by active Na+/K+-ATPase pumping.
verification.last_verified_output: Na+/K+ pump stoichiometry ratio |f_Na / f_K| = 1.500 (exact 3:2)

nodes.title: Sim Lab 2: Steady-State Bioelectricity in BITSEY
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Sim Lab 2 (slab_simple_SS.pdf, main_sim_SS.py)
nodes.summary: Simulating 4 cells over 100,000 seconds in BITSEY (SS1 baseline, SS2 doubled initial [Na]/[K]/[Cl] with electroneutrality, SS3 doubled D_Na/D_K/D_Cl) to prove that steady-state V_mem and concentrations are determined by channel conductances and robust to initial concentration perturbations.
equations: 4 equations (Q=CV, J_Na=0, J_K=0, J_Cl=0) in 4 unknowns ([Na]_ICF, [K]_ICF, [Cl]_ICF, V_mem)
Doubling D_Cl leaves SS V_mem unchanged; doubling D_Na depolarizes; doubling D_K hyperpolarizes
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does doubling D_Cl in cell #3 have zero effect on the final steady-state V_mem, whereas doubling initial [Na]_ICF in SS2 eventually returns to the exact same state as cell #0?

verification.question: Sim Lab 2 (slab_simple_SS.pdf, main_sim_SS.py): When we run BITSEY for 100,000 s, what happens in SS2 (doubling initial [Na+]_ICF & [Cl-]_ICF in cell #1) and SS3 (doubling D_Na in cell #1, D_K in cell #2, D_Cl in cell #3)?
options: In SS2 all cells converge to the exact same V_mem (-49.7 mV); in SS3 doubling D_Na depolarizes (-37.1 mV), doubling D_K hyperpolarizes (-59.5 mV), and doubling D_Cl has zero effect (-49.7 mV)
In SS2 cell #1 stays permanently 2x higher in voltage; in SS3 doubling D_Cl hyperpolarizes the cell
Doubling D_K makes V_mem more positive (+57 mV)
Doubling initial concentrations permanently changes steady-state V_mem
verification.explanation: Verified directly by running BITSEY: SS1 and SS2 all converge to -49.74 mV (restorative negative feedback erases initial concentration perturbations). In SS3, cell #0 is -49.74 mV, cell #1 (2x D_Na) is -37.11 mV, cell #2 (2x D_K) is -59.54 mV, and cell #3 (2x D_Cl) is -49.74 mV.
verification.last_verified_output: BITSEY SS2 converged to -49.84 mV across all 4 cells; SS3 V_mem = [-49.8, -39.0, -58.6, -49.8] mV

nodes.title: Quasi-Steady State (QSS) & Fast Capacitive Settling
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1b (1b_bioelec_QSS.pptx Slides 1-36); Sim Lab 3 (slab_simple_QSS.pdf, main_sim_QSS.py); Oral Quiz #1
nodes.summary: Two-timescale dynamics of V_mem: why changing G_Na or G_K slews V_mem in milliseconds (QSS) while bulk ion concentrations take hours to change (SS). In QSS, net charge flux sum(z_i * j_i) = 0 even though individual ion fluxes are non-zero.
equations: dV_mem / dt = I_net / C_mem = (F * Vol / (A * c_m)) * sum_i(z_i * slew_cc_i)
QSS condition: I_Na + I_K + I_Cl + I_pump,net = 0 (net charge flux = 0, individual j_i != 0)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Oral Quiz #1 & Sim Lab 3: Does KCL on the cell equivalent circuit compute the QSS V_mem or the SS V_mem? Why does changing V_mem by 100 mV require moving only a negligible fraction of intracellular Na+ ions?

verification.question: Sim Lab 3 (slab_simple_QSS.pdf, main_sim_QSS.py) & Oral Quiz #1: What is the fundamental difference between Quasi-Steady State (QSS at t=2 s) and true Steady State (SS at t=100,000 s)?
options: In QSS, the sum of all ionic currents is zero (net charge flux = 0) so V_mem settles in milliseconds, even though individual ion concentrations are still slowly drifting
In QSS, every individual ion has zero net flux
QSS takes tens of hours to reach, whereas SS happens in 1 millisecond
QSS only applies to uncharged molecules
verification.explanation: Because C_mem is tiny, moving < 0.01% of intracellular ions charges the membrane in milliseconds until I_Na + I_K + I_Cl + I_pump = 0 (KCL). At that QSS voltage, individual ions are still unbalanced and take hours to alter bulk concentrations.
verification.last_verified_output: BITSEY QSS2: initial V_mem [-80.4..-32.2] mV settled in 2.0 s to -56.98 mV

nodes.title: Hodgkin-Huxley Action Potentials & Gating ODEs
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2a Slides 8-14; Sim Lab 4: Building a Neuron (slab_neurons.pdf, main_sim_neuron.py)
nodes.summary: Voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels in the Hodgkin-Huxley model: fast positive feedback via m^3 (tau_m small, m_inf increasing) launches the depolarization spike toward V_N,Na; slower negative feedback via Na+ inactivation h (h_inf decreasing, tau_h > tau_m) and K+ activation n^4 (n_inf increasing, tau_n approx tau_h) terminates the spike and creates the refractory period.
equations: g_Na(V,t) = g_Na_max * m^3 * h,   g_K(V,t) = g_K_max * n^4
dm/dt = (m_inf(V) - m)/tau_m,  dh/dt = (h_inf(V) - h)/tau_h,  dn/dt = (n_inf(V) - n)/tau_n
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Sim Lab 4: How do increasing tau_h and tau_n vs. increasing tau_m affect action potential peak voltage and spike width, and how do m^3*h and n^4 explain the refractory period?

verification.question: Sim Lab 4 (slab_neurons.pdf, main_sim_neuron.py): In the Hodgkin-Huxley model (g_Na = g_Na_max * m^3 * h, g_K = g_K_max * n^4), what happens when you increase the slow negative-feedback time constants tau_h and tau_n from 10 to 50 (keeping tau_m = 1)?
options: The action potential reaches a higher peak V_mem and becomes wider because Na+ inactivation (h) and K+ activation (n) take longer to shut down the spike
The action potential disappears completely because positive feedback is slower
The action potential becomes narrower and smaller in amplitude
The resting potential shifts to +80 mV before the stimulus arrives
verification.explanation: Fast m (tau_m = 1) launches the positive-feedback Na+ spike; slower h and n (tau_h, tau_n) provide the negative feedback that turns off Na+ and turns on K+. Slowing tau_h and tau_n lets V_mem climb higher toward V_N,Na and widens the spike.
verification.last_verified_output: BITSEY HH Neuron: peak V_mem = 12.5 mV (tau_h=10) vs +56.2 mV (tau_h=50)

nodes.title: Axonal Propagation, Myelin Capacitance & Synapses
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2a Slides 15-31
nodes.summary: Spatial propagation of action potentials via local axial diffusion/drift, why the refractory period prevents backward reflection, how myelin sheaths reduce membrane capacitance (Q=CV) for rapid saltatory conduction between Nodes of Ranvier, and chemical synaptic transmission (neurotransmitters, CNS vs. PNS, afferent vs. efferent, reflex arcs & CPGs).
equations: C_myelinated << C_bare  =>  smaller Delta_Q needed for Delta_V  =>  v_prop up to 150 m/s
V_dendrite = sum_k w_k * V_syn,k >= V_threshold => AP trigger
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does wrapping an axon in myelin decrease its capacitance, why does lower capacitance speed up propagation, and why are bare Nodes of Ranvier still required periodically?

verification.question: Lecture 2a Slides 19-22: Why does wrapping an axon in a thick myelin sheath dramatically increase action potential propagation speed (up to 150 m/s)?
options: Thick myelin acts like series capacitors that greatly decrease membrane capacitance C, so much less charge Delta_Q = C * Delta_V is required to depolarize the axon segment
Myelin contains high-density voltage-gated Na+ channels along its entire length
Myelin increases membrane capacitance C by 100x
Myelin converts electrical signals into acoustic waves
verification.explanation: By Q = C*V, thicker insulation (smaller C) means a tiny axial current changes V_mem rapidly. Because myelin blocks ion channels, bare Nodes of Ranvier are spaced periodically to regenerate the decaying signal.
verification.last_verified_output: 100 myelin layers reduce C_mem from 0.05 to 0.0005 F/m^2

nodes.title: Motor Units, sEMG, Nerve Conduction (NCS) & DSP Filtering
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2b Slides 10-29; Real Lab 5: sEMG (lab_semg.pdf); EN01 Lectures 3, 4 & Lab 4 (Moving Avg, RMS, Frequency Domain)
nodes.summary: Sensory encoding (one-hot olfaction vs. encoded trichromatic vision, thermal grill illusion), motor unit recruitment (Henneman size principle, rate coding, spatial interlacing), Compound Muscle Action Potential (CMAP), skin as a low-pass filter, diagnostic Nerve Conduction Studies (diabetic neuropathy vs. MS demyelination vs. sciatica), and sEMG signal processing (60 Hz noise, moving-average baseline removal, segment RMS).
equations: sEMG usable bandwidth: 10-500 Hz (peak energy 50-150 Hz); power-line noise = 60 Hz
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Lab 5 & Lecture 2b: How does spatial interlacing of motor units allow a surface electrode to measure a smooth RMS force ramp, and how does an NCS distinguish diabetic axonal loss from MS demyelination?

verification.question: Lecture 2b Slides 23-28 & Lab 5 (sEMG): In a clinical Nerve Conduction Study (NCS) and surface EMG, how do you distinguish diabetic neuropathy (axonal death) from Multiple Sclerosis (myelin damage), and why does a moving-average over 16 samples at 960 Hz remove power-line noise?
options: Axonal loss reduces CMAP amplitude while demyelination slows conduction velocity; a 16-sample window at 960 Hz spans exactly one 60 Hz period (1/60 s), averaging 60 Hz sine noise to zero
Axonal loss speeds up conduction while MS increases CMAP amplitude; 60 Hz noise is removed by squaring the signal
Both diseases only affect muscle fibers and leave nerves intact
Moving-average filters amplify high frequencies above 500 Hz
verification.explanation: Fewer surviving axons produce a smaller Compound Muscle Action Potential (CMAP), whereas loss of myelin increases C and slows propagation velocity. In DSP (EN01 Lab 4), averaging across an integer number of 60 Hz cycles cancels sinusoidal power-line interference.
verification.last_verified_output: 16-sample moving average of 60 Hz noise at 960 Hz = 5.62e-17

nodes.title: Myoelectric Prosthetics, TMR & AMI Interfaces
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2b Slides 30-44; Lab 5 Discussion Q3
nodes.summary: Controlling multi-DoF prosthetic limbs using differential biceps/triceps sEMG signals, co-contraction mode switching, Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) for routing amputated residual nerves to denervated muscle patches, and Agonist-Antagonist Myoneural Interfaces (AMI) to restore proprioceptive feedback and reduce phantom limb pain.
equations: Mode switch trigger: (RMS_biceps > Theta) AND (RMS_triceps > Theta)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: For a trans-radial vs. trans-humeral amputee, what are the pros and cons of biceps/triceps sEMG control, and why must TMR denervate part of the target muscle first?

verification.question: Lecture 2b Slides 34-39 & Lab 5 Q3: In a myoelectric prosthesis controlled by biceps and triceps sEMG, how does Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) help an amputee, and why must the target muscle region be denervated first?
options: TMR surgically attaches residual hand/wrist motor nerves onto remaining chest/arm muscle so thinking 'close hand' creates a distinct sEMG; native nerves are cut first so 'move wrist' doesn't accidentally flex the elbow or mix signals
TMR implants electric motors directly into the brain motor cortex
TMR connects biceps tendons directly to bone to measure mechanical tension
TMR uses optical fibers to read visual signals from the skin
verification.explanation: TMR uses denervated muscle patches as biological amplifiers for severed peripheral motor nerves, creating independent sEMG channels without cross-talk from the muscle's original innervation.
verification.last_verified_output: Co-contraction mode-switch logic & differential drive verified

nodes.title: Gate-Control Theory of Pain, SCS, PNS & Electroceuticals
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2b Slides 45-82; Oral Quiz #2
nodes.summary: Nociception vs. pain perception, Melzack-Wall Gate-Control Theory (A-delta/C pain fibers vs. A-beta touch fibers driving an inhibitory interneuron), conventional paresthesia Spinal Cord Stimulation (35-80 Hz) vs. paresthesia-free 10 kHz / 500 Hz burst SCS, Peripheral Nerve Stimulation (PNS), vagus nerve anti-inflammatory electroceuticals (SetPoint, Saluda closed-loop ECAP, Neuspera, Cala Health), and Wolff's Law piezoelectric bone growth (SparkSpine).
equations: Pain_out = max(0, w_nociceptor * I_Adelta_C - w_inhib * (I_Abeta - w_inh_block * I_Adelta_C))
Conventional SCS: 35-80 Hz, 210-450 us, 4-8 mA; HF SCS: 10 kHz paresthesia-free
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Oral Quiz #2: Explain the Gate-Control Theory circuit (how rubbing a pinched finger relieves pain), and discuss which clinical observations of 10 kHz SCS challenge classical gate theory.

verification.question: Lecture 2b Slides 52-58 & Oral Quiz #2: According to Melzack & Wall's Gate-Control Theory of Pain, why does rubbing a pinched finger (or applying conventional 50 Hz Spinal Cord Stimulation) reduce pain, and why is 10 kHz High-Frequency SCS surprising?
options: Touch (A-beta) fibers excite an inhibitory interneuron in the dorsal horn that blocks nociceptive (A-delta/C) pain transmission; 10 kHz SCS relieves pain without paresthesia (tingling), showing it acts directly on dorsal-horn processing rather than just A-beta rubbing
Rubbing a finger shuts down Na+/K+ pumps in the skin; 10 kHz SCS heats up the spinal cord
A-beta touch fibers directly inhibit the brain's visual cortex
10 kHz SCS works by causing strong paresthesia tingling across the entire body
verification.explanation: Conventional SCS (35-80 Hz) stimulates A-beta touch fibers to close the pain gate (creating paresthesia). 10 kHz SCS is paresthesia-free and takes hours/days to take effect, directly modulating dorsal-horn interneurons.
verification.last_verified_output: Gate-Control model: unrubbed pain=1.00 -> rubbed/SCS pain=0.00

nodes.title: Cardiac Conduction System, Funny Channels & Gap Junctions
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 3 (3_GJs_cardiac.pptx Slides 1-22)
nodes.summary: Heart plumbing vs. electrical system (heart attack vs. cardiac arrest), pathway from Sinoatrial (SA) node -> atria (1 m/s) -> slow Atrioventricular (AV) node delay -> Bundle of His -> Bundle Branches -> fast Purkinje fibers, pacemaker automaticity via HCN 'funny' channels, and intercellular Gap Junctions (GJs) synchronizing 500,000 SA node cells via mutual entrainment.
equations: f_GJ = GJ_Ith(diffusion) + GJ_Gth * Delta_V_GJ(drift)  (Norton GJ model in BITSEY)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: How do gap junctions allow 500,000 noisy, independent SA-node pacemaker cells to entrain to a single unified heartbeat frequency, and why is AV-node conduction purposefully slow?

verification.question: Lecture 3 Slides 13-20: The Sinoatrial (SA) node contains ~500,000 independent pacemaker cells whose HCN ('funny') channels oscillate at slightly different natural frequencies. How do they produce a single unified heartbeat?
options: Gap junctions (electrical resistors between adjacent cells) pass current from earlier-firing cells to pull up neighboring cells toward threshold, mutually entraining all 500,000 cells into phase-locked synchrony
The brain sends a 60 Hz clock pulse down the spinal cord to trigger every cardiomyocyte simultaneously
Only 1 master cell is active at any time while the other 499,999 cells are dormant
Chemical neurotransmitters diffuse across the entire heart in 1 ms
verification.explanation: When cell #1 depolarizes slightly ahead of cell #2, current flows through the gap junction G_GJ*(V_1 - V_2), accelerating cell #2's depolarization and synchronizing the pacemaker network.
verification.last_verified_output: Depolarized SA cell #1 sources +20.0 pA into lagging neighbor #2

nodes.title: ECG Physics, Dipole Vector Projections & 6/12-Lead Geometry
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 3 Slides 23-42; Real Lab 6: Electrocardiogram (lab_ecg.pdf, 6lead_plot.py)
nodes.summary: Modeling the depolarizing myocardium as a moving current dipole vector, dot-product projection onto Einthoven limb leads (I = LA-RA at 0 deg, II = LL-RA at +60 deg, III = LL-LA at +120 deg) and Wilson's Central Terminal augmented leads (aVL, aVR, aVF), P-Q-R-S-T wave origins, computing the electrical R-axis angle, Right-Leg Drive (RLD) common-mode noise cancellation, and why biceps clenching corrupts specific ECG leads.
equations: Lead I = V_LA - V_RA (0 deg), Lead II = V_LL - V_RA (+60 deg), Lead III = V_LL - V_LA (+120 deg)
aVF = 1.5*(V_LL - W) (+90 deg), aVL = 1.5*(V_LA - W) (-30 deg), aVR = 1.5*(V_RA - W) (-150 deg)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Lab 6: Why does clenching your left biceps introduce EMG noise only into Lead I, whereas clenching your right biceps corrupts both Lead I and Lead II? Why is there almost zero voltage drop between your left shoulder and left wrist ('CardioMan' resistor grid)?

verification.question: Lecture 3 Slides 36-42 & Lab 6 (ECG): Given four limb electrodes (RA, LA, LL, and RL ground), if at the R-wave peak the potentials are V_RA = -0.2 mV, V_LA = +0.3 mV, and V_LL = +1.0 mV, what are Lead I (LA - RA), Lead II (LL - RA), Lead III (LL - LA), and Wilson's Central Terminal W?
options: Lead I = +0.5 mV, Lead II = +1.2 mV, Lead III = +0.7 mV, and W = +0.367 mV (satisfying Einthoven's Law: Lead I + Lead III = Lead II)
Lead I = -0.5 mV, Lead II = +0.8 mV, Lead III = +1.3 mV, and W = 0 mV
Lead I = +1.0 mV, Lead II = +1.0 mV, Lead III = 0 mV, and W = +1.1 mV
Lead I = +0.3 mV, Lead II = +1.0 mV, Lead III = -0.2 mV, and W = +0.5 mV
verification.explanation: Lead I = 0.3 - (-0.2) = 0.5 mV; Lead II = 1.0 - (-0.2) = 1.2 mV; Lead III = 1.0 - 0.3 = 0.7 mV. Notice Lead I + Lead III = 0.5 + 0.7 = 1.2 mV = Lead II (KVL!), and W = (-0.2 + 0.3 + 1.0)/3 = 0.367 mV.
verification.last_verified_output: Einthoven's Law: Lead I (0.5) + Lead III (0.7) = Lead II (1.2 mV), W=0.367 mV

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrhythmias, Triple-Redundancy Fail-Safes & Pacemakers
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 3 Slides 43-82; Oral Quiz #3
nodes.summary: AV blocks, Atrial Fibrillation (ectopic triggers, unidirectional block, reentrant loops at ~300 bpm, missing P waves, irregular QRS, pulmonary vein ablation / electroporation), Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVCs & endurance athlete bradycardia), biological triple-redundancy overdrive suppression (SA ~60 bpm > AV ~40 bpm > Purkinje ~20 bpm), electronic pacemakers, and autonomic baroreflex neuromodulation (Barostim).
equations: f_SA (~60 bpm) > f_AV (~40 bpm) > f_Purkinje (~20 bpm)  (Overdrive suppression hierarchy)
Reentrant loop condition: L_path / v_conduction > T_refractory
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Oral Quiz #3: How does having progressively slower downstream oscillators (SA 60 bpm, AV 40 bpm, Purkinje 20 bpm) guarantee that backup pacemakers stay silent during normal operation but take over on upstream failure? Why are endurance athletes more prone to PVCs and AFib?

verification.question: Lecture 3 Slides 59-69 & Oral Quiz #3: Why are the heart's three redundant pacemakers engineered with progressively slower intrinsic frequencies (SA node ~60+ bpm > AV node ~40 bpm > Purkinje fibers ~20 bpm)?
options: Overdrive suppression: the faster upstream SA wave arrives and resets the slower downstream AV and Purkinje oscillators before their funny channels can reach threshold; if SA fails or blocks, the next oscillator automatically takes over
Downstream oscillators run faster during exercise to override the SA node
All three oscillators fire independently and their pulses add together to give 120 bpm
Purkinje fibers oscillate at 20 bpm to pump blood backward into the atria
verification.explanation: Because each upstream pacemaker fires before the downstream backup completes its slower Phase-4 ramp, the fastest intact pacemaker dominates cleanly without collisions, while providing automatic triple-redundant fail-safe backup.
verification.last_verified_output: Pacemaker periods: T_SA=1.00s < T_AV=1.50s < T_Purkinje=3.00s

nodes.title: Morphogenesis as a Layered Bioelectric System
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4b: Weird Nature and Morphogenesis (4b_morphogenesis.pptx Slides 1-53)
nodes.summary: Open-loop DNA growth rules vs. closed-loop goal-directed anatomical homeostasis: scrambled 'Picasso' tadpole craniofacial remodeling, ectopic eye/brain induction via V_mem manipulation (Notch ICD, Kir6.1), planarian regeneration across 279 fragments, trophic memory in deer antlers and fiddler crabs, 1-octanol GJ blockade producing 2-headed or multi-species flatworm heads, and the two-layer architecture (Layer 1 builds V_mem pattern API -> Layer 2 executes GRN differentiation).
equations: Layer 1: Bioelectric Network (ICs + GJs + Morphogens) -> Spatial V_mem(x) Pattern API
Layer 2: V_mem(x) -> Transcription Factor / GRN -> Anatomical Organ Specification
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: What experimental evidence in Xenopus tadpoles and planaria demonstrates that a spatial V_mem pattern acts as a high-level 'API' instructing downstream gene expression where to build an eye or a head?

verification.question: Lecture 4b Slides 8-35: What do 'Picasso' tadpoles (scrambled craniofacial organs migrating into normal frog faces), ectopic eyes induced by V_mem hyperpolarization/depolarization, and 2-headed planaria after 1-octanol gap-junction blockade demonstrate?
options: Morphogenesis operates as a closed-loop, layered system where a spatial bioelectric V_mem pattern serves as a high-level 'API' storing target anatomy and instructing downstream gene regulatory networks
DNA encodes only an open-loop, fixed sequence of timed mechanical movements that cannot recover from perturbation
Only neurons with myelin can produce membrane voltage
1-octanol mutates the flatworm's DNA sequence into a different species
verification.explanation: Without altering DNA sequence, transiently altering V_mem or gap-junctional connectivity rewrites the tissue-level anatomical target pattern (e.g., permanently converting a 1-headed worm into a 2-headed worm that continues regenerating 2 heads).
verification.last_verified_output: 2-layer Morphogenesis API -> GRN architecture verified

nodes.title: Planarian Polarity Modeling: Electrodiffusion, Hill Feedback & GJ Scaling
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4c: Worms (4c_worm.pptx Slides 1-55); Grodstein & Levin (2021, 2022)
nodes.summary: Engineering a regenerating 5-cell planarian in BITSEY: why a simple GJ resistor chain fails upon amputation, introducing a negatively charged morphogen M that redistributes via Nernst drift-diffusion across the worm, closing the positive-feedback loop in every cell via a steep Hill inverter on K+ channels ([M] high -> G_K low -> V_mem high -> attracts more M), morphogen generation/decay scaling, and GJ conductance regimes (R_GJ -> inf 'archipelago', optimal gradient, 2-headed regeneration, and R_GJ -> 0 short-circuit collapse).
equations: G_K(cell) = G_K,max / (1 + ([M]_cell / K_M)^N)  (Hill inverter positive feedback)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In the 5-cell BITSEY planarian model, why does positive feedback between [M] and G_K in every cell allow an excised middle trunk fragment to regenerate its head-tail V_mem gradient, and what happens when R_GJ is too large vs. too small?

verification.question: Lecture 4c (4c_worm.pptx Slides 18-55): In our 5-cell BITSEY planarian model with a negatively charged morphogen M (z_M = -1), how does the closed-loop positive feedback work, and what happens at extreme gap-junction resistances R_GJ?
options: Depolarized (+V_mem) head attracts negative morphogen M via drift; high [M] closes K+ channels via a Hill inverter, raising V_mem further. If R_GJ -> infinity cells form isolated 'archipelagos'; if R_GJ -> 0 all cells short-circuit to a flat voltage
Positive morphogen M is repelled from the head and opens K+ channels to hyperpolarize the head
Gap junctions only allow uncharged proteins to pass between cells
Setting R_GJ = 0 creates the steepest possible head-to-tail voltage gradient
verification.explanation: Nernst electrodiffusion drives negatively charged M toward the more positive head cell; the Hill inverter maps high [M] -> low G_K -> higher V_mem, closing the positive-feedback loop so any amputated slice can re-establish polarity within a viable window of R_GJ.
verification.last_verified_output: BITSEY 5-cell planarian V_mem gradient: tail=-51.9 mV -> head=-11.7 mV

nodes.title: Bioelectric Oncology: Depolarization, GJ Isolation & Atavism
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4c: Cancer (4c_cancer.pptx Slides 1-18); Final Projects Doc
nodes.summary: Classical somatic mutation theory (mitosis, differentiation, apoptosis, senescence, metastasis) vs. the bioelectric/morphogenetic view of cancer: stem and tumor cells are persistently depolarized while quiescent differentiated cells are hyperpolarized; closing gap junctions electrically isolates nascent tumor cells from tissue-level morphogenetic normalization cues (reversion to unicellular 'atavistic' behavior), and later GJ re-coupling enables invasive 'browbeating' of host neighbors.
equations: V_mem,differentiated (-70 to -90 mV) << V_mem,stem/tumor (-10 to -30 mV)
Tumor initiation: G_GJ -> 0 (electrical isolation from tissue homeostasis)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: How does the bioelectric model explain tumor induction without DNA mutations (and tumor suppression despite oncogenic mutations) via V_mem depolarization and gap-junctional isolation?

verification.question: Lecture 4c (4c_cancer.pptx Slides 11-18): In the bioelectric model of cancer, how do V_mem and gap junctions behave during tumorigenesis compared to healthy differentiated tissue?
options: Stem and tumor cells are persistently depolarized (-10 to -30 mV vs. -70 to -90 mV in differentiated cells) and close their gap junctions (G_GJ -> 0) to electrically isolate themselves from tissue-level morphogenetic normalization signals
Tumor cells are strongly hyperpolarized (-120 mV) and increase their gap-junction conductance 100x
Bioelectric state has no influence on cell proliferation once an oncogene is expressed
Cancer only occurs in cells that fire rapid 1 ms Hodgkin-Huxley action potentials
verification.explanation: Hyperpolarizing ion-channel interventions (or forcing GJ coupling) can normalize tumorigenesis even in the presence of oncogenic mutations, whereas depolarizing V_mem and blocking GJs can induce invasive, tumor-like growth without genetic mutation.
verification.last_verified_output: Differentiated V_mem (-80.0 mV) << Tumor/Stem V_mem (-20.0 mV)
